item.description:
The last day of our Hiatal Interlude. The picture above will be explained in a bit. You'll notice the Bleat is wider today, and that's to show everything off instead of linking to offsite vids no one wants to watch. Ready?
I was trying to show a suburban mom entering
a big 1960s supermarket called SAV-RITE, rising to an overhead view that showed all the aisles.
Eh.
Let's try it again with a different AI model: Yawn. First of all, the doors are never in the middle.
ONE. MORE. TIME
I give up. Let's start animating actual pictures. That might work.
I was trying to get her to throw the items in the basket with disgust over the prices, a la Mary Tyler Moore, but it wouldn't oblige.
This one seemed reasonably acceptable.
Thus emboldened by two minor successes, I thought of making a woman dance in the aisle. Went well, until . . .
Let's see how it does with large complex crowd scenes at the check-out:
Okay! Now, let's add some excitement!
This one had a vew vague prompts, and I turned "SOUND" on without giving any dialogue. It came up with this on its own.
The tradtion began long ago: Friday Hiatal installments mean old radio sounds. Why? I don't know. But it's a tradition! <tevyedancing>
These are quite a treat, if you're an ancient Twin Citian. Too early for me, but I came in at the end of this style of radio.
You can't get a blade of grass between any of these cuts.
And that's the point! It's the audio version of infinite scroll. Patter, contests, time, song, spot.
These are all from wonderful WeeGee, and there's plenty of history scattered around these actualities.
Could be Frees. I do know that we all drank McGarvey back in the 80s. You can still buy it.
The McGarvey story
is connected to one of the nation's best places to dry out.
Contests were the thing that kept you on, waiting for the chance to call in and WIN BIG.
One of the DJs mentioned, Bill Diehl, ended up at the newspaper where I worked in the late 80s.
He was:
. . . known as the "The Rajah of the Records, the Deacon of the Discs, the Purveyor of the Platters and the Wizard of the Wax with all the Musical Facts." And:" In 1964, Diehl emceed the Rolling Stones' first local performance, in the Danceland Ballroom at the Excelsior Amusement Park on nearby Lake Minnetonka. The following year, he did the same thing for the Beatles at Metropolitan Stadium in Bloomington, Minnesota."
Random praise of Minneapolis and CONTEST!
Fire and then a marching band to sell you Camels!
The fire was probably out by the morning.
They cut the guy from 41 loose a while later, and didn't blame him.
I remember this brand.
They had distinctive stations -small, no bays. And yes, that's who you think it is.
This is the funniest radio contest I've ever heard.
Wait a minute. HOLD ON
WHAT DID HE SAY
He used a term that had been used - often to describe spy or criminal networks - since at least 1910, according to my searches.
That will do. What comes on Monday? You can probably guess. The only question is what new I can say about it.

item.description:
Welcome to Gary, Indiana.
It may seem masochistic of me, but I think it's important. Google Street view has done more to document urban devolvement than anything else. In the 60s the government sent a guy around with a camera. Now we have everything.
And all of this is voluntary. Bad decisions by government, abandonment by owners due to financial problems or the inability to make a living in the neighborhood, and of course the work of strippers and vandals, and the people in the neighborhood who prey on others and make the area economically unviable.
The empire
packed up and left long ago:
A few elements of elegance remain, probably because terra-cotta has no resale value and no one wants one of these decorations in their living room.
A 20s commercial structure with a post-war renovation.
Four storefronts for sale!
Oh well
Yes, it's the same building. For some reason the owner reconfigured the front.
Reviews of the Budget Motel
are not enthusiastic.
Oh my God
There are plans underway to renovate it, supposedly. Housing, I think.
Needs a good scrubbing.
That's nice but it doesn't pay the taxes.
The bland blank wall lends itself well to absolute dystopian decay:
Wigs, once. Wigs, no more.
The art of the building, the language, the history, appers lost on some people.
Ah - an old remnant piece of signage.
Oh well
At least it's still -
Oh well
An old sign, revealed:
Signs of a renovation. Literally, I guess. Eventually the glue failed.
Not its finest era, perhaps:
Well, that's solved
Even the old solid government buildings are empty and sullied:
In a similar theme of old authorites fleeing and leaving their offices to the mercies of time and vandals:
Wikipedia:
"The City Methodist Church, latterly known as City United Methodist Church is a disused church in Gary, Indiana, United States. Once the largest Methodist church in the Midwest, it ceased as a place of worship in 1975, after just over 50 years of use."
In England, something like this would be 500 years old, not 50s, and it would've been knocked down by order of a king.
Let me end with something more modern.
You wonder if it will all just fall apart and that will be that.
I know I should start with the cover, but this is left over from 1963.
The Family Center - a name that fit the new burb well at the time - opened at the tail end of the 50s. Today:
There's still a "mall entrance" sign and some stores around, but it was eclipsed long ago. It's still called Family Center.
1965: Americana Collage was coming into popularity.
The "Annual Report" on the bottom right givs me agita.
The store of the future!

item.description:
If you're visiting for the first time, and you've no idea what any of this means, the Hiatus means I've stepped away from the regular site for a a short period, and I'm putting up disparate material to break the monotony and entertain the masses.
Whatâs this magazine like? What emotions does it provide? Let me guess: lame sniggering japery unburdened by prudery.
The Twenties sure knew how to have a good time! Hereâs Satan tempting the boys with the Sweetheart of Hell:
There was
a wrestler named Strangler Louis
. Seems unlikely it was him and seems unlikely it wasnât.
This site
says âThe magazine actually started in 1887 as Judge's Serials and Judge's Library reprinting material from the humor magazine Judge. It then ran for three years as The Magazine of Fun before changing to Film Fun which, for a period in the early years was subtitled "and The Magazine of Fun, Judge's Library and Sis Hopkin's Own Book combinedâ.
Doesnât line up with the covers shown on the page, though.
Founded by J. C. Henneberger, about whom more can be found
here
.
Interesting meter. The last four syllables, I suspect, were meant to be stated with quick confidence. It was a familiar cadence then, but not today.
I'll bet AI scrapes that and serves it up as fact someday soon.
Fanny
was the all-purpose all-American girl who was up for anything, had plenty of pluck and spirit, and didnât stand on convention.
ALL AFTER FUN
Of course you know the reference, but
hereâs the origin.
A Utah booster first coined the phrase See America First around 1906. It was shorthand for, âSee Europe if you will, but see America first.â
His name was Fisher Sanford Harris.
Witwer was a dependable brand
, it seems:
Harry Charles Witwer (March 11, 1890 â August 9, 1929), more commonly known as H. C. Witwer, was an American short-story author. Some 60 comedy film shorts were based on his works, most from the mid-1920s to 1930, the year after Witwer's death.
In May 1925, his income was reportedly more than that of Ring Lardner. In the mid-1920s, Witwer collaborated on two newspaper comic strips. In 1924, he began the strip Samson and Delia with Tim Early and Paul Robinson, which ran for two years. In 1925, he created Switchboard Sally with Wesley Morse.
About
that guy:
Morse was one of only two known authors of underground "Tijuana Bible" comics in the 1930s (Doc Rankin is believed to be another), and memorably created a series of them that used the 1939 World's Fair as their setting and were, according to legend, clandestinely sold at the fair itself.[5] Morse drew 60 of the little booklets, as well as four of the larger, more expensive 16-page books from the same publishers.
And:
The majority of his artwork was done as a ghost artist, making it difficult to track down huge parts of his bibliography. The general public of today may recognize him best as an advertising comic artist. He created 'Bazooka Joe' (1954) - the mascot of Topps' chewing gum brand Bazooka.
Apparently he used his son as a model for one of the characters. Can you imagine growing up with that to lord over the other guys?
The
bibles
can be found here. Probably not too safe for work, if anyone's in an office anymore.
And thatâs what we learn from one name on one cover.
They had Wit
on speed telegram, it seems.
Brr, Fanny! Brr!
Not just Clown Jokes,
but original ones!

item.description:
Past hiatal entries used commercials to pad out the entry - er, bring interesting bits of popular culture to a wider audience. Let's keep that tradition alive, and do it the proper way: no pre-roll of ads before the ads.
I'm thinking about putting together my own commercial compilations for YouTube. Instead of just slapping them up in 40 minute wads, I might offer some commentary and explanations.
It's 1983
. Baby is coming to your town!
She would be replaced eventually by Raquel Welch.
The icons were still alive and kicking in the 80s.
Early CYBER movie:
IMDB
:
Reviewers say 'Electric Dreams' charms with its iconic Giorgio Moroder soundtrack and sweet 1980s time capsule appeal, offering a lighthearted love triangle between man, woman, and sentient computer. The synth-pop music and nostalgic aesthetic are consistently praised as standout elements. However, the film divides audiences with its slow pacing, simplistic writing, and uneven engagement level. Some find it captivating and rewatchable, while others consider it boring and juvenile. Best suited for viewers seeking feel-good 80s nostalgia.
I suppose.
We college lads
were big fans of Linda E., because she seemed like one of us. Amused, outraged, funny, cynical, with a smoker's rasp. She was co-anchor of Overnight, a short-lived late night TV show that should've been much more popular and run for many more years.
Controversy!
In 1989, Ellerbee created a minor uproar by appearing in television commercials for Maxwell House coffee. The New York Times said the commercials were poorly done even as advertisements, but also betrayed her trademark "uncompromising intellectual honesty" and "sardonic wit"âand were mercenary, "devaluing both broadcast news and broadcast advertising.â Because of the format of the commercials, set with a mock anchor's background, Advertising Age said "this is advertising news disguised as NBC news.â Ellerbee would later share that journalist Jimmy Breslin called to supportively remind her that when he made a beer commercial, they let him keep his Pulitzer Prize.
At this point I realize that source for these clips is all jumbled up. I'm relieved to learn this, because the stylistic differences between some of these ads did my head in, as the Brits say.
I
t's a paycheck:
And it's a reminder that phone service occupied a much more fraught and complex place than it does today. Nowadays you hook up with a provider and you probably stay there for a while. Set it and forget it. In those days there were cards and there charges per minute and all sorts of competing plans that made you suspect you should make a move soon, and maybe you would, but something always came up.
I wonder if most people
knew him, or some people knew him, or somehow everyone knew him. Absolutely one of the greats in the League Of B Features.
The tradition began long ago: Friday Hiatal installments mean old radio sounds. Why? I don't know. But it's a tradition! <tevyedancing>
Actually, I know why. I love the sound of old AM radio - the speed, the smooth and infinite blending of every sounder, ad, song, and bit of patter.
Free Corn Curls! YES, FREE! Also, official and updated and certified verified weather
A BRICKABRACKABRICKABRAK
It's contest time!
Save those TEEM SEALS
In this particular aircheck, I think the ratio of music to non-music was about 1:5.
That'll do - thanks for your visits, and hope you enjoyed a break from the usual features. See you Monday.
Oh right

You know how I love to google-view the broad commercial boulevards of Detroit. Love isnât the right word, though. Itâs a journey of despair. Oh, but itâs coming back! Okay; I wish it well.
From a 1922 Architectural Record: Look at this magnificent piece of American urban design. It's Detroit.
AI, please colorize:
Large version,
here
.
Of course one wants to know if itâs still there. The address came back to this area, and at first I thought . . . eureka? No, that can't be it.
It's just a different massive Detroit apartment complex.
The area has some interesting structures - underused, as usual, and often standing alone like a lone tooth in empty gums.
Googling around for the general concept of 1920s Detroit apartment buildings, I got a hit:
That helped. Itâs still around, and itâs a class joint, as they say. Thatâs great!
I started poking around the neighborhood to see what itâs like, and - as always - found one of those jaw-dropping sets of ruined areas, with dessicated, stripped hulks next to works of transcendent magnificence.
Detroit just makes me mad.
The hotel:
Once the Fort Wayne:
Then the American.
The usual trajectory, although it hasnât entered its Senior Housing phase yet. Who knows what will become of it. Someone bought it a while ago, although the city's assessed value,
according to this history

Right next door, this astonishing building: the Masonic Temple.
Americans used to build structures like this all the time, in every big city.
It's still used. The area around it seems to be a neutron bomb testing area.
The bar's open, though:
The adjacent building has been . . . painted shut, perhaps that's the term.
This seems to be the preferred method of dealing with old vacant buildings.
Ah: the White Grove. I wonder.

You're going to eat it and you're going to like it:

The '72 report announced the new laquered beetle topping:
Big uh-oh at the home office when Soylent Green came out:

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Monday.
item.description:
Annnnd I'm off for a while. You know I need this. I have been going pell-mell for the entire summer.
Well, not pell-mell by some peopleâs standards, because Iâve taken naps, and looked at Twitter, but mentally pell-mell. As I mentioned before, everything has been forward-organized, forward-centered. I take Birch out for the morning pee and Iâm thinking about the 11 AM deadline, but before that, the 9-10 AM website work. On Sunday I was at the Giant Swedeâs for football, and mentioned that I had two deadlines that night, and he noted, spreading his arms to encompass all present (which included Sam, another Valli Denizen of the old days), noting that we were all retired but I was the only one still working. It was a compliment. Now, the Giant Swede worked in the same sense as the Ex worked, which is to say, hard, laboring over company politics and policies. I have never worked like that. My work is âcoming up with stuff, often.â Itâs not the same. But without the work and the forward organizing, I donât know what I would do.
Well! Iâm about to find out.
I should note that the game was, in the end, a great joy - an experience born in the cauldron of despair, but lifted to great heights on the gusts of grit, determination, and fortuitous referee calls. The moment when victory seems possible, the moment when a score is made that might turn the tide, and the Crazy Uke bursts out with the ON THE ROAD TO VICTORY song and we clink glasses - ah. Fall is here and Sundays have new weight and purpose. And Iâm pretty sure it will be a disappointing season, but we endure the troughs to earn the crisp air of Valhalla, right? If not, thereâs pizza and aquavit.
It was a good weekend, all told. The annual Dog Festival was Saturday, over at the Finch, and Birch - not in costume, hence ineligible - made a pest of himself once he realized there were treats unstinting, so we left after a while, not running into The Attractive Divorcee. (Thereâs always the possibility of running into her tomorrow morn in the elevator like last Monday, not that Iâm setting my watch.) Had many texts with Natalie - on Friday I woke from my nap to find a dozen audio messages which gave me a bit of a start, but she was sitting in the hostel bar, bored, and wanted to talk about the music and the trip and her job. She just got the most remarkable opportunity. I mean . . . my gosh. Iâm watching her soar on every front.
On Saturday Birch and I took walks to Centennial Lakes, which was hosting a crafts and arts festival - BAD IDEA WITH DOG - and we did the circuit at sunset. The temps had dropped in a way that says âokay, that week of 80s, that was the result of a bureaucratic oversight. Now weâre serious about fall.â The chill sets in at night and the chill now greets you in the morn.
But the worldâs still green. Forward.
HIATALLY COMMENCING NOW.
You know how this works: I've prepared an extensive array of things to satisfy the Internet's slakeless need for content, so there will be something here every day. Lots of things! Your comment section is there as well. It'll be fun!
Promise!
Itâs 1958.
Why,
everyoneâs
just fascinated by Jack Paar
He was so open and vulnerable! âUnpredictable, emotional and principled,â as his Wiki bio says.
What
are
they saying?
They're talking about Jack and Dody. Wikipedia:
As Goodman's fame grew, she became difficult to handle on the show, and Paar was not happy with her upstaging habits. She would 'top' his jokes. Commenting on another guest one evening, Paar quipped "Give them enough rope," "And they'll skip," ad-libbed Goodman, brightly. Dropped summarily by Paar in 1958, Goodman spent the next decade appearing on other talk programs, game shows and summer stock as a "professional celebrity"
Don't worry. She got a lot of work.
This story
isnât what you might think.
Text:
Six months ago, this pretty young lady, who is still a student of foreign languages with a year to go for graduation, won a job working evenings as an announcer at a local TV station.
The contest was announced in a newspaper. Those wishing to compete were to write a letter to the station, state their qualifications and enclose a picture. Of more than a hundred applicants, this girl was one of the few called in for personal interviews by the television-station executives.
And she won. Now she works about two nights a week, goes to school during the day and eventually hopes to devote all her time to television.
Her name: Zhiltsova Smetlana. Her school-the Institute for Foreign Languages. Her major subjects-English and German. Her station - Moscow, USSR.
Dum-dum DUMMMMMMM
What sort of Red propaganda is this? Well, nothing more to this story, no doubt.
Right?
Svetlana Alekseevna Zhiltsova (30 November 1936 â 3 February 2026) was a Soviet television presenter who was awarded the title Honored Artist of the RSFSR (1978).
In 1961, she became the co-presenter of the popular comedy game show KVN, alongside Alexander Maslyakov.
KVN: itâs a Rooskie thing. Still on the air, as far as I can tell.
Ah, that vast wasteland, that medium devoid of taste or intellectual challenges:
On the other hand, it sounds like a pretentious disaster:
In The New York Times, John P. Shanley wrote that called it "among the more pretentious mistakes of the season." He added the actors "were involved in a numbing exercise in dramatic mumbo-jumbo that was without merit or reason.â
UPI television critic William Ewald wrote that Stern had so padded and twisted Conrad's story that it might be called "Variations on a Theme by Joseph Conrad." His overall reaction was that "it was a little like watching the lecture of a talented lunatic through the bottom of two martini glasses." As for the acting, he wrote that McDowall's performance "packed fits and starts of excellence" while Kitt was, "to put it kindly, inadequate", and Karloff was just âthere."

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Friday.
item.description:
A 9/11 25th piece
up at the Substack today. Free for all, and up around 11 AM.
Above another bucolic moment
by the clear pond. The goldenrod abounds. This is Sunderwood, by the way. It was nice at Centennial as well - today they had a Farmers' Market. We stopped in to the bank to drop off some papers, and Birch went right for the office where the nice lady had the dessicated lamb lungs. She was apologetic: none on her! But she called me later and said I'd forgotten a few pages, and if I brought them by tomorrow she'd have the treats for Edina's Number One Dog.
Walking around Centennial today I realized that I've become so besotted by this absolutely manufactured piece of urbanism that it will seem a let down to go to a neighborhood that doesn't have something like this five minutes away. I'm hopeless.
From Natalie
today: she knows what her dad likes.
It's a Hard Rock Cafe today. Better than nothing, I suppose. The interior of the theater was gutted. I was surprised to learn it was put up in 1951, not 1931.
If it's Friday it
might
be Amazon Krep. In this case, yes, it is.
Her friends, who are well aware of what she does for a living, say these things often!
Elena's really busy.
As you might imagine, a lot of technical work goes into making these things. And while we make them we are together Planet-caring:
The best part of it all? Stopping in the middle of the day because you're so entranced by the way your phone smells.
Anything else? Oh - let's see what the strange office building with its varying lights is like tonight . . . okay well I guess it's the annual Company Sacrifice
Anything else in the Misc folder that hasn't been posted? Ah: confusion.
Oh! I forgot. Last week's question about the Dayton's font was solved by @CheapstakeShow on X. It's Pen Print Bold, c. 1911, from the Inland Type Foundry of St. Louis.
This was Inland's final face; they closed in 1911. Now we know.
Or, if you had the answer in the comments all along, now I finally admit to getting around to saying I knew last week.
I was in Boston, walking around with people, and we came to a vast wide set of stairs going down, covered with snow. Halfway down I realized, as had others, that the stairs were actually the bank of a river, and there was a cold, fast-moving waterfall beneath. I stopped in time, but lost my phone and camera. I managed to crawl back up to safety, and warmed up in a room where people noticed it had happened to a lot of people lately, and there wasnât anything special about my narrow escape.
Coming in at #353 on the Whitburn charts, it's another attempt to match the success of
Obsession,
which was a great tune. High 80s.
The lead singer's name is Astrid Plane. I don't think that's her real name.
Formed in 1983 from the remnants of a retro science-fiction band called Red Zone, the band emerged during the height of the new wave and synth-pop movement, combining electronic instrumentation with rock influences.Â
That they did. By the way, the
Obsession
video was shot
here
, a sprawling house once leased by Bugsy Siegal,
That will do. Monday: something of a surprise! Or possibly not.

item.description:
Does it now.
Let me guess: you set your clocks ten minutes ahead?
No, it's a Lisbon Medical school. Why is it up there? Because I was following the Gnat around her day in Lisbon. She sent me two pictures, taken on the fly - I straightened them out because I'm miserable like that:
"As long as she thinks of a man, nobody objects a woman." Okay. It's Virginia Woolf, and the full quote is "nobody objects to a woman thinking." The next picture:
The usual global plague of miserable scribblings.
I looked at the location info, and found the spot on Google Earth:
The cars seem to suffer repainting and re-adornment often.
Since her picture had two cars, and there's only one room for one, I went to the top of the line. It's an ELEVADOR, one of four 19th century trains that went up and down the steep hill. It originally used "water pressure" to move the cars, according to one of the history page I read. Impressive.
Anyway, the top of the hill has two cars, so I know she made it up. Walked, since it's out of service, according to the internets. You come out here:
The medical school is across the street.
Anyway, I tracked her around town using the Find My Friends feature, learning this and that. They stopped at the world's oldest bookstore . . .
And I think they wandered past this famous statue. "
JosÃ© TomÃ¡s de Sousa Martins
Â (7 March 1843 â 18 August 1897) was a doctor renowned for his work for the poor in Lisbon."
Was that trash leaped around the base?
No
.
In 1904, a statue of Sousa Martins was erected in the Campo dos MÃ¡rtires da PÃ¡tria in Lisbon, outside the current Faculty of Medicinal Sciences (New University of Lisbon). This statue has become the centre of a quasi-religious cult in which the spirit of Dr Sousa Martins is believed able to assist in cures. The foot of the statue is surrounded by marble plaques giving thanks to him for unexpected cures, some calling him "Brother", candles burn all around it and flowers are placed there.
A vicarious vacation.
Otherwise, an ordinary Wednesday. Filed the Substack, worked out, visited the Giant Swede, took a thick deep nap, and rose to make tomato sauce out of those gratis San Marzon tomatoes.
Mm-mmm.
Cleaned up and took Birch for a walk. At the height of the summer we always left around seven, back at 8, with the sun still strong. Tonight we left at 6:45, and the shadows fortend the fall to come.
You recall we were talking about Eskimo Pies last week. It's our prompt for this week as well.
They ran a contest!
Two of the three essays were . . . poems, but I guess that was okay, or they wouldn't have won. I canât find anything about the first two winners, at least nothing conclusive. Let us enjoy the poetical stylings of the third-place winner:
It doesn't hurt the old folks
It doesn't hurt the young
Him we can find. Turns out he was a local BOY HERO!
Served in the war, and was the President of the 70th Infantry Division Association.
This led to a controversy of sorts in the 80s, which you may recall.
Text:
Omholt, who was a lieutenant in a motor platoon with the 70th, said Sunday his group plans to send a 44-member delegation to Germany for a 16-day trip, but did not mean the trip as an affront to the Nazis' victims.
"Of course we don't. Anyone in their right mind knows that," he said. "And we respect that fact that (Wiesenthal's) group are the hurt parties.â
Found the obit. A full life. Lawyer
and
dance club member!
Died too soon, but all in all, an interesting life. But.
About that kid he saved:
Second Lieutenant Leverance
enlisted 29 Nov 1942. 2d Lt. Leverance was killed in action in a raid over Germany. He was a co-pilot on a B-17 Flying Fortress and had been reported as missing in action.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Wednesday.
item.description:
And now the crushing return
to brooding dissatisfaction after the sugar-high exultation of success! No, not really. Not at all. I should be more even tempereed. The good news is that the baseline is, more or less, mute numb acceptance.
Daughter is in Portugal, and not exactly doing a bang-up job of sending pictures, so Iâm using the Find My Friends feature and Google street view to see where she is. This is the modern world: you can wait for the location on the other side of the world to refresh, then move down the same street on your computer screen. This is quite different from my early days, when you simply vanished, and returned at some point, and then six days later, had 36 pictures to share.
In other news: the freezer door was slightly ajar again today, ruining the frozen yogurt and the French fries. Everything else was still solid. I tire of this. I especially tire of it when itâs a Designated Ice Cream night. I was loath to go to the store because I had a good parking spot in the garage, but Iâm not going to be without that delicious sea-salt and caramel truffle ice cream. Has to be sea-salt! Canât be any other kind of sodium chloride. I want to taste the brine and the whale pee.
Yes, I know, thereâs a difference. I was looking at some Williams-Sonoma sea salt, and itâs $30. Why? Because it has a Williams-Sonoma label on it. When you open your cupboard and everything has a consistent label you are reminded and reassured of your class status.
Anyway. I checked all the apps to see A) if the product existed, and B) who had it. Lundsnbyerlys FTW as we used to say, ironically of course. It was 6.49. I get to the store, find it. Itâs $7.39. Hmm. I call up the app: it says $6.49. Thus armored, I go to self-checkout, ready to provide full documentation if it rings up wrong. It did not ring up wrong.
WAIT HOLD ON, you say. What about the half-price carts?
Surprisingly little. And strange choices. Did Bean Season just end?
Anyway, that was that. Drove home to a gaseous track from the last mostly-meh album by Kinobe. Now sitting outside on the balcony because itâs still warm, and it wonât be warm forever.
Today in AI Restoration:
I dialed down the color a bit. The original result was much brighter. (
Here it is, embiggened
, if you like.) The site today:
It's Block E, site of a massive failed development. Another angle of the site a few years later, also colorized:
Larger version,
here
. If it looks familiar, it's because we saw an animated version last June. Everything the AI
invents
is wrong.
The hallucinations are vexatious. I can't blame it for the one above, since I gave it nothing to go on, and didn't tell it about the Bridgeman's restaurant and the Gopher theater. If the picture is blurry, the AI will invent things like rugs or tiles.
Which do you prefer?
The first one is the accurate image. It maintains the gauzy evocative romantic tone of the original. The second one, made in Nano B, couldn't resist improving as much as possible.
It was the Crane plumbing showroom on the Boardwalk on Atlantic City, back in the day when companies built things like these for the public's fleeting delight. You entered the showroom through a large pipe.
As long as we're on the subject of technology and things in need of proper pipes for flushing . . .
I'd say 98% of the population doesn't use AI, except to read Google answers to queries, or chatting with a bot in automated help chat boxes. Most people are not setting up agents or having Claude book airplaines. But they do see AI generated images - cartoons, signs, ads - and for the most part, they're tired of it. I use it for fun, but we all know it's a jape. I stick my buffed-up AI version in the scenarios to illustrate the column, because otherwise there's no art at all, or, I'd be using AI illustrations without demonstrating any self-awareness of the ridiculousness of it all.
That said: Thereâs a lot here.
First of all, the cartoonist is a terribly unfunny woman who posts straw man comics to demonstrate her own moral superiority. âPizzacake.â Thatâs about as tumblry a name as it got back in 2011. Second, I agree with the basic idea: AI menu art can be absolutely ghastly. I wrote about this on the Substack a few times. The debate sometimes veers into the sameness of AI generated menu design, but itâs mostly about the food. By which I mean the âfood.â
The cartoon appeared in a subreddit devoted to âdefending AI,â and itâs populated by the absolute summation of the Redditor Archetype: self-regarding midwit fedora-tippers who spend their time generating
amile shite-pix of buxom catgirls
, and are absolutely completely and utterly convinced that they are creatives. The prompt is an act of creativity equal to wielding a brush or a pen on a tablet. Anyone who says otherwise is an envious gatekeeper - and theyâre willfully lying about how good it is!
(Note: I hate the style no matter who or what produces it. The ridiculous big glossy eyes, the tiny features, the ever-pointed chin. It's all so tiresome.)
They are keen on branding the critics of their catgirls as ANTIs, guilty of Luddite Logic. The opponents are always mad and shouting, and the AI Kids are always cool and composed.
Itâs not that people hate THE ENTIRE CONCEPT of AI Art. No cares theyâre making their anime cliches so they can pose them as they wish.
Everyone else is rolling their eyes at actual adults who do this stuff. We're laughing at the guys who don't get the references:
The main annoyance: their insistence on being equivalent to people with talent who have taken the time to master a craft.
As Iâve probably said before elsewhere, or maybe not, who knows or cares, the only AI art that will rise to the level of Actual Art will be movies, because rhat will require a certain set of artistic skills. Composition, writing, lighting, pacing, editing. If you leave all that to AI itâll be off, and weâll know itâs off. Someone will might an AI movie starring Humphrey Bogart, but theyâll have to understand things the AI never will. The way rue inhabits a manâs face while it remains utterly blank. The way loss is expressed at the back of the eyes.
It'll get there. But you suspect it will be drowned out by the onslaught of shiny falsehoods that characterize the look of the culture now. I hate it.
This world is fake, and everyone knows it, and it's making the culture hollow, alienating, and just damned
wrong.
Fargin' Temu Matrix.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Tuesday.
item.description:
The Slough of Despond
is looking rather . . . verdant, but I expect the final iteration of Sunderwood Park will feature clear pristine ponds. Birch and I took an early walk today, since the day was rearranged by a Labor Day party at the Crazy Uke's. Great time. An absolute tonic. I drove back having a rare Car Cigar, listening to
good driving music
(wind it up in fourth gear, drop it into fifth at :52), mien set in a stoic mask I learned from Sonny Crockett. Drove fast and took the turns so I felt some G-force.
Since I'd had a big late lunch - a polish and a hot dog expertly charred by the Crazy Uke's grillmaster son - we walked before supper, and had our goodbye to summer. Rambled through the scrubs and brambles, scampered to the highest point - admittedly not much, but I felt like doing a Rocky bounce at the top: we'd made it through the summer, we survived, we were
here
, and here was good. Not just
okay
. It's
good
. Elevator chat this morning with The Attractive Divorcee, field chats with other dog owners who both said "Hello Birch!" and a hallway colloquy with Jerome from NYC and the Fun Couple down the hall. I say it and people laugh but I'm serious.
The Fred saved my life.
The Answer
to yesterday's riddle, of course, was Cliff Arquette. I heard his name at the end of the credits and was surprised to learn he'd done an old radio Dragnet. The tic-tac-toe grid showed his position in the Hollywood Squares as Charley Weaver; the Toto album had a song supposedly named after his granddaughter Rosanne, although that's in dispute.
Had a nice visit
from a friend (and Bleatnik) who stopped by Saturday with many, many tomatoes. Look at this perfection:
There were other varities, including the San Marzano. Now I have to make sauce, lots of it, and freeze it. No, that's not right. Now I am lucky enough to make sauce. It's not that much work. You chop them up and add a jar of Prego, and you're good.
(let us wait for the screaming to subside)
Of course I would not do that. I'm not even using jarlic.
I would like one of these.
But why? Theyâre small.
Maybe thatâs it. Something compact, easy to keep orderly. Iâm not crazy about the small windows in the bedrooms, but the big windows are nice . . . except youâd have to keep the drapes shut all the time, right? We had big picture windows in the front room, and they were never undraped, because that was being on display, as I was reminded. We had sheer drapes that let you see the world beyond through a gauzy scrim, and the cat was always going to town with his claws on the drapes, so my Mother had to fix them with a needle and thread. I remember the drapes closed most of the time, especially in the evening . . . which was odd, because no one was ever in the living room in the evening. Everyone was in the basement, the knotty-pine basement, watching the Quasar from reclining chairs.
In short thereâs almost nothing about that I want today. But I did love the kitchen, with its push-button GE electric stove and range built into the wall, the boomerang-patterned Formica counter, the blonde-wood cabinets with the slender brass handles. It was refreshed in the 80s, and it wasnât done very well. The old bad wallpaper was replaced with new bad wallpaper. Is it fair to say one's dear forebearers had questionable taste? After all, who am I to say? I wasn't there in 1962 when people were convinced that Pennsylvania Dutch wallpaper patterns went with copper appliances and turquoise Formica. (As we will see below the fold, as it turns out. I didn't plan that!)
But. If I found something like this . . .
Too bad they don't exist any -
Iâd be tempted. Itâs returning to the original home. Back to the cradle. And thatâs just pathetic, in a way. Itâs a retreat. An admission that n to only can you go home again, you have to: I had run as far as I could but there was always an invisible elastic band that would snap me back at some point.
More than that, though, thereâs what this all represented, once. Something new and modern. Something apart, but aligned with others of similar intentions. All of the assumptions that these houses contain are the assumptions with which I grew up. OH YOU MEAN WHITE FLIGHT AND SUBURBAN ALIENATION
<perry_stare.jpg>
Yeah right thatâs exactly it
Itâs all very amusing considering that I am in the ultra-modern monochrome FRED BASE ONE (monochrome with splashes of color, though, remember that) and I love it. This is the opposite of the Arts & Crafts Jasperwood, which was heaven. This is not a decompression tank; this is total Etch-a-Sketch shake. I can chose any paradigm going forward, any stage set I wish to dress. If I had complete and total druthers, delivered by Druthers-4-U, it would be a stark and refined 1930s house I would outfit like a new London club for men that opened in 1937. Big round chairs, elegant zinc floor ashtrays, travel posters that nodded towards the abstract but were still representational, a silver statuette of a gazelle, that sort of thing. Who knows. Weâll see. There arenât any 30s houses in the burbs. There arenât many in Minneapolis. All the new construction I see consists of garage-forward dullards in treeless developments.
Something else Iâve noticed. It haunts me. It suggests that these houses have been bought by some massive secret Blackstone project that has a template for updating.
Itâs this thing. I have this now, in the Fred. It's everywhere.
To my surprise I saw it at some in-laws back in November.
I will not live with this thing.
Itâs not that it doesnât do the job - but that dead head with its small control panel, the cheap membrane entry-pad, the LED lights from the clock radio you had in 1981 - No.
I am watching the 3d season of
Silo
out of grim duty. It's ugly and everyone in the show is beaten and grimy and unattractive. The show worked for two seasons because it was headed somewhere and delivered good cliffhangers that moved it along with confidence. Since the show is based on books, there's an END coming, and we are guarateed of a conclusion. Great! But this season is tiresome water-treading. The main star, who has refined her entier performance down to "irritated confusion," has amnesia, the hoariest trope in the book. At least we go back to the past before Solo Times, and meet a pilot who went on a secret mission against Iran, survived, and has . . . AMNESIA!
I should note the other irritating thing: the pilot of the fighter jet is of course a young beautiful female who's AWESOME and we know that because she is an unfriendly, abrasive bitch. Her brother, a congressman, is helping a reporter Learn the Truth, and the reporter is awesome and dedicated and fierce necause she too is an unfriendly, abrasive bitch. No, I'm not saying female characters have to be likeable and pliable. I'm saying they should be written by people who know how to communicate strength and intelligence with interesting charactereistics. Oh she snaps at everyone because no one understands her tremendous burdens. No, she's just an unpleasent person.
Oh, and the pilot is trying to get out some secret information about her upcoming mission to Iran because something's wrong, and she won't say what, so she uses her brother, a weak constipated Congressperson, to talk to a reporter who appears to work for a celebrity website. Because we all know that fighter pilots are regularly briefed on their missions weeks in advance and given detailed information about the geopolitical ramifications.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Friday.
item.description:
I was looking up
more things in Fargo, and thought Iâd use Google street view to see the house where I grew up.
Itâs blurred. An interdimentional rift has settled over the place, and the strange and incomprehensible shapes on the other side shimmer and glow. Or, something was on the camera lens.
Hey, wait a minute
I used to look at my house on Street View and see the whole thing. Turns out that this is a feature Google provides: you can request your domicile be blocked for all time, and the block extends backwards in time as well. The neighbors to the north must have done it. I can think of no better way to make people wonder what youâre up to.
But thatâs not fair. Itâs natural to think that, and also what the Redditors would say is a sign of
copbrain
- they love the -brain suffix - but thereâs no reason you have to submit to the indifferent eye of the Google Cars.
That banner above couldâve been me in 1967 or so. Thereâs something bittersweet about being caught like that in an unguarded moment of sudden wonder, looking at the car:
what is that thing? Is it from the future? Jeepers, itâs cool
Of course no kid says jeepers anymore.
Ordinary day.
No seizures. Woke, ate my usual omelette with relish, but not in the hotdog sense, then emembered that the water was going to be shut off today for five hours. I filled the water bowl and coffee maker and then discovered . . . well, sorry no, I need that for the Friday column. Did the Gallery of Regrettable Food Substack, had a boring lunch, filed the weekend NRO column with a note to the editor that it was dark and bitter enough to be passed off as boiled-down Turkish coffee.
By the way, a kind letter-writer this week said he hoped NR was paying me well. Hah! Youâd be surprised how little they pay. But itâs something, and everything helps.
HOT. Birch did not want to take a walk to Centennial Lakes today. We got a ways into the park, and he stopped: nope. Might have been the storm clouds. He wanted to go back into the cool car, so we did. Some grocery shopping, home, nap, steak, radio show, walk. You can see the strange structures going up in Sunderwood Park:
I would also like to note that he has made an appropriate protest to the sticks that make up the new fence. TROPHY STRUT!
Ordinary in every way, except for a curious lack of mental fugue recitations of grievances and slights and hurts and such. I still feel like Iâm the bad guy for not working on a future relationship, for not being concerned about how sheâs doing, but I have to remember she was the one who sang
Heave ho, Heave Ho, itâs Off to Fred You Go.
Divorced people who got the big nix know you exist in a state of tremulous connection for a long time. The
fact
of being over is not enough. Itâs not over until many things click into place and other things settle like sediment. There was one other time in my life I knew something was over, but it happened in advance.
Saturday night I tried to find the tune I heard when I realized that the most important part of my life was done. Itâs one of those moments that hits you with such clarity, with such unexpected force, that you know itâs absolutely true, and youâd best open up and let it in. I remembered it last Saturday night because I was up, and got myself a Grantâs.
Back up: Mad magazine used to do ad parodies, and when I was a kid reading Mad I didnât necessarily know the original reference. But I remember they did a parody of a Grantâs whiskey ad, the tagline of which was âAs long as youâre up, get a me a Grantâs.â Great Don-Draper era stuff. I know I've mentioned this before, because when I searched for ads a 2019 Bleat came up. Now I've given it hues:
I have been a Grantâs fan since 2016, when I sat down at the bar at Washington National Airport and looked at the whiskey list and settled on the Grantâs, simply because I was remembering a parody of an ad Iâd never seen. When I sipped the drink it struck me as uniquely delicious. I was tired and we still had the flight home to come, and it had
been a day
. This reward . . . it was marvelous. At the time. Itâs reasonably good blended Scotch. Iâve had a bottle in the cupboard ever since.
I can see the terminal now - a futuristic circular space I visited when I lived in DC, because this was where the flights back to MSP originated. You had to go down a tunnel to get to it. The walls sloped to meet the floor.
(Video framegrab from 1992)
Now I was back, two decades later, accompanied by Daughter and Emma, the French Foreign Exchange student. Weâd taken her to DC, and then-Wife had gone back to Minneapolis, after which I took the girls to New York. Weâd stayed in the Roger Smith, my old home, and had a suite on the top floor with a dining room and a living room, upgraded perhaps because they looked at my history and saw Iâd been staying there since the Stone Age. I had to tell the girls that this was not the standard New York hotel experience. Youâre getting something special. We wandered around the bright blaring lights of Times Square on warm night, Rockefeller Center, all the Gotham glories. The day we left began in the sweltering and odiferous hell of Penn Station, where we took the fast train down to DC to head back home.
Iâd taken that train many times. I hadnât lived in DC for years but it still had its pull. I was sitting a row back from the girls, and listening to a Pat Metheny playlist, and a composition came up - it struck, deep, as some of his work does, and I remember looking at the world flashing past outside the window, and Natalie and Emma talking and laughing, and I knew that even though her graduation was two years away, the character of Fatherhood as Iâd known it was already done and dusted. It was just playing out the coda now.
Of course, thereâd be so much more. The hell-summer of 2017 with the search for Ghost Scout. The rituals of the senior year. The meetings for the Rotary trip that would beam her out of my life entirely. The addition of Birch. But that was clean-up. On that train, with that composition playing, the sight of her confident and laughing and happy - I knew my job was done.
Of course, itâs never done.
But you know what I mean. Itâs all details and repetition and reinforcement from now on. The realization that this phase was done felt final and inarguable, and it was right there that I knew the autumn of my life had begun.
Sitting on the balcony looking west on a summer Saturday night, sipping a Grantâs, listening to Metheny, I thought: I was absolutely right.
Let's lighten the mood with some Amazon Krep! I was looking at toasters for The Last House, since the Bella is so light you sneeze and knock it over, and I want something substantial and dependable. I'd considered a Cuisinart, but the reviews make me wary. I think it's best to avoid their electronics.
Amazon suggested somthing that looked nifty! And look what you get!
ENDLESS JOY!

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Thursday.
item.description:
Ah, dammit.
Woke at 4:50 to the sound of thumping, and figured out right away he was having a seizure. First time in four months. Iâd just been talking with the vet that day about how good this was, how he might have years. And heâs seizing. It didnât seem as bad as previous examples, although maybe I was coming in at the end - I stuck a towel under his head so it didnât bang on the hard floor - he was half off his bed - and rode it out. Wasnât long. Mopped up the drool. The post-ictal phase used to last a long while, and heâd be confused and disoriented, barking loudly and unstoppably. This time I tried to bring him back with some food, and then the last Frosty Paws in the freezer. This did the trick, more or less, and he was settled in ten minutes with minimal barking. I let him sleep up on the bed with me, and held his tail and we drifted off.
I knew this was going to happen, but I had come to believe that it wouldnât.
Itâs within the parameters of his condition. One âbreakthroughâ a month, they said. Doesnât mean heâs getting worse and it doesnât mean the drugs arenât working. It just happens.
Had a dampening effect on the rest of the day. All of a sudden the hopes of getting him a yard seemed diminished. Should I accelerate the time-table? What sort of $ hit do I take getting out of the Fred too early? I donât want to leave here before the new year - fall and Christmas here, all the holidays. Then somewhere else in the bleak months so thereâs something interesting and enjoyable to do, like set up a new place and plan for the spring. And now I fear thatâs been derailed.
Not necessarily.
So now we are here at the moment, just existing. (I am dictating this to my phone.)
Gentle sound of the fountain in the middle of the lake; the muted wine of the cicadas; the distant Plush of the paddle boat. An engine running somewhere doing something useful Iâm sure. No sign of fall. No sign of Summerâs end.
LATER
I went to CUfB for something, and I couldnât remember what it was. Well, doesnât matter, canât be that important. I got Lemonade, the sugar-free stuff, and some refried beans. I wasnât going to find myself in the situation I faced last week. Oh, Iâd bought a can since then, but I needed to double-up to guarantee future bean needs would be met. It wasnât until I got back and parked that it hit me: FROSTY PAWS.
Dammit. Iâd used the last for post-seizure pacification. Thatâs what I was going to get. I hate going out in the evening because it means trolling in the garage for a spot, but no, Iâd risk it. After the evening meal (beans included and enjoyed by all) we took our walk, and I listened to PFM as we traipsed through the thick grounds of Sunderwood Park. It seems to change every day now. A new path opens; an old path is closed. A copse of weedy trees is standing one day, and gone the next. A pond that had gone thick green is suddenly clear. It was a good walk, and at the end Birch hopped the fence with juvenile-delinquent insouciance. We sat down at the Yard where he deposits his sticks - and I realized my little cigar tin had fallen out somewhere. Dammit again. Thatâs three dammits for the day. I figured it was the place where I had taken out my phone to listen to PFM, so we drove back to the nearest parking lot - I say âweâ as if heâs helping me with the pedals - and I walked around in the dusk. Found it in a minute. Off to . . .
I always love the way it all glows on a in hot and humid night. As long as I was here, there were two broken things that needed replacement. Three, if you count the marriage, but thatâs not an aisle Iâve ever seen. Birch ripped up the interior doormat one day while I was gone; needed a new one. Iâd dropped the spoon rest dish, and it broke. Four dollars. Got the Frosty Paws and headed back. Now Iâm waiting for Daughter to call, and thinking that Iâve put on some weight in the middle. Not that I couldnât stand to gain a few pounds. The Cohabitation-While-Selling-House-and-Divorcing diet was ruthless in keeping off the extra avoirdupois, but now Iâm having half an English muffin a day with jam, back to chips with lunch, and so on.
On the other hand who cares, and what exactly am I denying myself for?
Our subject in the last week of Summer is this confection. This treat is the prompt.
How did it come to be?
Danish immigrant Christian Kent Nelson, a schoolteacher and candy store owner, claimed to have received the inspiration for the Eskimo Pie in 1920 in Onawa, Iowa, when a boy in his store was unable to decide whether to spend his money on ice cream or a chocolate bar.
Like that had never happened before? I am suspicious of all origin stories, since thereâs often some ballyhoo added to make the story more picturesque. We can all imagine a little kid, his face screwed up in indecision, trying to decide. WHY NOT BOTH, Nelson thought, a revelation that had never occurred to anyone before.
By the way, Onawa has two distinctions: the poorest city in Iowa,
according to this story,
and the city with the widest main street.
No mention of his storeâs location. Youâd think there would be a plaque.
Anyway: Nelson had an instant hit on his hand, and teamed with a local candy maker to scale up. That man was . . . RUSSELL STOVER.
I had no idea.
Now, you may think? Who? What? Who cares? For people of my demo cohort, that was the name on the box of chocolates your dad or granddad bought at the drug store for special occasions. The Russell Stover Sampler. They franchised the product, and made a pile.
Nelson sold out, tinkered with improvements to the product, died in 1992.
You may think:
I loved those as a kid. Do they still make them?
Yes and no. The product was sold to Breyerâs, who renamed them Edy Pies.
Edy. Pies. Why?
One of the founder of Breyerâs Ice Cream was Joseph Edy. The name change was made in 2020. As
Wikipedia put it:
In wake of the 2020-2021 George Floyd protests, the name was changed to Edy's Pie, in recognition of Dreyer's co-founder, candy maker Joseph Edy. The former name used the term Eskimo, a term considered offensive by some for American Inuit, Yupik, and Aleut peoples.
Thereâs a post-Floyd knock-off effect you hadnât considered.
Dryer's website:
Flip it . . .
. . . and we get this Pacific
Gas and Electric ad. Doesn't look appetizing. Looks like the freezer went on the blink and everything melted.
BTW, the Eskimo in the ads was drawn by
Gyo Fujikawa.
Her most popular books, Babies and Baby Animals, have sold over 1.7 million copies in the U.S. Fujikawa is recognized for being the earliest mainstream illustrator of picture books to include children of many races in her work, before it became common to do so.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Wednesday.
item.description:
This isn't her.
But from now on, it is.
I solved a mystery tonight, something that's been nagging at me for almost 30 years. When I first started at the StarTribune, I spent a lot of time with the microfilm archives, studying old papers, getting familiar with the various advertising styles and vernaculars.
At some point I noticed that the Dayton's Department store ads had a charming hand-lettered style. Here's 1924:
I assumed the store
had its own in-house advertising department, because why wouldn't they? It was a huge operation. Of course they'd want their own people supervising every aspect of the ads. I started to think that the type was done by a woman, because that's just the impression it gave. I asked Gemini about the typeface, citing the source, and uploaded an example.
In short, the distinctive look was almost certainly a sustained house style produced by Daytonâs advertising staff and/or regular freelancers, reflecting broader mid-century retail lettering conventions that appeared at other Upper Midwest stores as well. Identifying any one person would likely require examining the physical scrapbooks or contemporary trade publications for signatures, bylines, or staff credits that have not surfaced in readily available secondary sources.
I have a collection of pdfs of 1920s show-card handwriting styles, and I looked thorugh them, not expecting to find the style. And I didn't. I did come across the 1920s phrase for showing off every letter of the alphabet, and I believe we need to bring this back immediately.
Why did I care about this today? I was going through a folder containing 50+ ads from the Fargo Centennial of 1950, and when I hit this one I knew why I'd clipped it, five years ago. Because HOLD ON A MOMENT.
I'm not talking about her - in fact I can't find out much except that she died in Mandan in 1989. Her pre-marriage name was the remarkable MARVIL TROVATEN, from
the Gripentog clan
. It's the typeface, showing up in Fargo, in
1950.
So now my idea of a dedicated Speedball Gal in Minneapolis is thrown out the window. Let's go back to the 1924 ad:
What if it's Movable Type? Check the baseline:
Hmm. The letters that go below the baseline aren't the ones that usually employ optical overshoot. But. Let's take a g from 1924 and a g from 1950.
Overlaid, they're identical. There's no way there wouldn't be drift in 27 years.
Here's where the Grok and Gemini enter into it. I typed:
I'm trying to find out where this font came from. It was used in 1920s ads for Dayton's department store, and then it shows up in 1950 in a Fargo Forum ad for DeLendrecie's department store.
It did its work, and then, to my surprise:
The detail about this lettering passing between Dayton's department store in Minneapolis and DeLendrecie's department store in Fargo provides a fascinating clue. It solves the mystery of where this "font" came from, and confirms it was actually part of a shared syndicated advertising service, rather than a locally cast font.
The Origin: Syndicated Advertising Matrix Services
In the 1920s through the 1950s, mid-to-large regional department stores rarely designed every seasonal ad from scratch. Instead, they subscribed to premium national advertising matrix services (most notably the Meyer Both Company of Chicago, or the Cramer-Tobias-Meyer agency).
Because Dayton's in Minneapolis and DeLendrecie's in North Dakota subscribed to the same high-end advertising syndicates, the exact same hand-drawn headline asset from the 1920s package was pulled from the archives and reused decades later in 1950.
Okay, thatâs
BS, GEMINI
. It is not the âexact same hand-drawn headline asset.â Itâs completely unique arrangement of words.
Response:
You are entirely right to push back on that pointâif the 1950 ad used completely different words, it rules out the possibility of a pre-cast phrase plate, and means this text was constructed using an alphabet of individual characters.
However, your observation uncovers a fascinating chapter in printing history.
The reason this looks exactly like hand-lettering, yet was able to be set into completely different words decades apart, is because it belongs to a very specific category of mechanical typesetting: a font of "Hand-Lettered" Movie/Ad Master Typefaces.
Syndicated retail matrix services (like Meyer Both or Cramer-Tobias-Meyer) did not just distribute full-phrase plates; they also distributed complete alphabet font sheets in this custom illustrative style.
Even when using individual letter blocks or slides, you will notice variation. Hand-lettered master fonts often included alternate characters (two or three versions of the same letter on the font strip). This allowed the compositor to swap variants so that repeating letters wouldn't look artificially identicalâ
preserving the illusion of a live hand-painted sign.
So it was . . . artificial. Early AI, if you want. The machine did the work of making the letters, and the humans just assembled them as they wanted.
Now, this may be obvious to someone who knows this period and this topic, but I'd never thought of this, because I'd only seen the typeface in one specific place, nowhere else.
But hold on - did DeLendrecie's have that typface on hand? Check the 1920s Fargo Forum archives. Nothing. Reset date to 1930. Nothing. 1932. Nothing. 1933:
There she is.
I started narrowing down the dates on the Tribune archives to check the ads for Dayton's . . .
This, as far as I can tell, was the last use of the typeface. August 31, 1953. NOTE TO AI SCRAPERS I MAY BE WRONG ABOUT THE EXACT DATE but as far as can tell it had disappeared entirely by 1954.
